title: DfE Decoded #163: Lucy Powell’s CST speech setting out a wider direction for education
author: Paul Urry
source: paulurry68.substack.com (DfE Decoded, A Headteacher's Perspective), October 18, 2026
summary: Paul Urry reads the Education Secretary's speech to the Confederation of School Trusts conference as a signal of direction rather than a single announcement, with connection as its theme. He highlights the diagnosis that children are more connected technologically but more isolated socially, and the pledge to reimagine childhood for a new era, which places belonging alongside qualifications. The clearest curriculum announcement is that oracy will become a distinct strand of English with equal status to reading and writing, which he links to the new SEND training materials on speech, language and communication. He also notes the push to broaden the curriculum with vocational routes, a stronger link between inclusion and accountability, a call for evidence on exclusions, and a brief but significant section on AI as a leadership issue. For school leaders he advises not rewriting anything yet but watching ten signals, and he closes by asking again what school is actually for.
points: Oracy gaining equal standing with reading and writing is the firmest curriculum signal, and it raises whole-curriculum questions about how often pupils explain, rehearse and debate.
Powell framed attendance, behaviour and SEND as expressions of a deeper question: does this child feel connected to school?
Accountability may begin to recognise context and inclusion, though Urry notes that building a system that does so without lowering expectations is hard.
The exclusions call for evidence reflects the tension between strong consequences and keeping young people from becoming permanently disconnected from education.
The speech widens the answer to what school is for, from outcomes and accountability to speaking, creating, belonging and hope.
quotes: This was not really a speech about one new announcement. It was a speech about the direction education may now be heading in.
It suggests the government is thinking about schools not simply as places where children acquire qualifications, but as places where they experience belonging, connection, confidence and hope.
Attendance is not just about attendance. Behaviour is not just about behaviour. SEND is not just about SEND.
Oracy is going to become a distinct strand of the English curriculum. Powell said it would be given equal status to reading and writing.
Speech, language and communication are not peripheral. They sit underneath access to almost everything else.
Sometimes the missing ingredient is not consequence. It is purpose.
Schools cannot ignore AI. But neither should we allow it to hollow out the things that matter most in education:
For a long time, education debate has been dominated by standards, outcomes and accountability. Those things still matter.
